title: The shadow-screen lab
subtitle: Spring 2 • Week 3 • Block, let through, explain
objective: Explain that a shadow forms where an object blocks light from a source.

sow.exactOutcome: Investigate how shadows are formed when light is blocked.
sow.alignment: Direct match to the named outcome. The lesson is a 40-minute exemplar, with optional greater depth; no accreditation completion is claimed.

priorLearning: Everyday objects can be described by what we observe.
Use a labelled diagram or evidence card to explain a choice.
success: Place a blocker between source and screen.
Explain a shadow using blocked light.
Use evidence to compare materials without overclaiming.

vocabulary.meaning: A darker area where less light reaches a surface because light is blocked.
Does not let light pass through.
Lets some light through, scattering it.
Lets much light through so objects can be seen clearly through it.

equipment: Low-power LED torch; white screen; card rectangle; clear plastic sample; translucent paper; stands; printed cases.
preparation: Pre-cut equal-sized samples with safe edges. Fix source, sample and screen positions.
Check that the screen shows a useful contrast with room lights comfortably on; supply the evidence cards if not.
safety: Low-power cool LED only, aimed at the screen below face level. No Sun, lasers or hot lamps.
Keep floor routes lit. No pupil works in complete darkness.
Use safe plastic, not glass. Do not place materials over a hot light.
practicalAlternative: Use the constructed observations and ray diagrams. Actual visibility varies with materials, lighting and source size.

misconceptions.claim: A shadow is a black object sent out by the card.
misconceptions.correction: A shadow is a region receiving less light because light is blocked.
misconceptions.check: Remove the card: what changes on the screen?

misconceptions.claim: Transparent materials can never cast a shadow.
misconceptions.correction: They can cause faint shadows or patterns; much light passes through clear material.
misconceptions.check: Use the cautious wording on card C.

misconceptions.claim: The shadow always has the object’s colours.
misconceptions.correction: An opaque object blocks light; its surface colours are not projected by this simple setup.
misconceptions.check: Compare two equal opaque shapes with different colours.

access.supported: Choose one route: short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed explanation; keep the same science goal.
access.standard: Use the evidence provided to record a decision and explain the science in short sentences.
access.stretch: Apply the same core idea to a changed setup, identify a limitation and justify a better decision.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence and equipment. Offer seated observation, a quiet paper route, partner rehearsal and a pass. Never require public performance or a darkened room.

slides.title: Build a screen silhouette
body: You need a clear dark shape.
slides.notes: Pose a stage-screen design brief. Pupils will choose a sample for a clear silhouette and explain how it works. No performance is required.

slides.title: Three clues for our design
body: 2. What does a surface do when it reflects?
slides.notes: Accept a valid source; reflection returns light from a surface; an opaque card blocks transmission. Explain that reflecting and blocking transmission can occur together.

slides.title: I start without a blocker
body: The source sends light to the screen.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I need a comparison. Before adding the card, I check that the source lights the screen. If it does not, I repair the setup before judging a material.”

visual.title: An open light path
visual.description: Three rays from a small light source reach a screen with no card in the path.

elements.text:
The screen receives light
from the source.

slides.title: I put a card in the path
body: Less reaches part of the screen.
That darker area is the shadow.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I trace the light towards the card. Some paths are stopped; rays past its edges still reach the screen. The shadow is on the screen, not a dark substance leaving the card.” Other room light can make it grey rather than black.

visual.title: Light is blocked
visual.description: Side-view light-ray model. Ray arrows point away from a small source. Boundary rays pass the top and bottom edges of an opaque card and locate the shadow on a screen.

elements.text:
Less light reaches
this screen area:
a shadow.

slides.title: Materials let different amounts through
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “I judge the observation in this setup. Clear plastic may still give a faint edge or pattern; I will not claim it can never affect light.” These arrows are qualitative, not counts of photons or measured percentages.

visual.title: Materials change the light reaching the screen
visual.description: Schematic comparison of opaque card, a translucent sheet and clear plastic. Arrow counts are qualitative, not measured percentages. Clear materials may still cast faint shadows.

elements.text: Same source, screen and sample position

slides.title: Choose a silhouette material
slides.notes: Constructed evidence comes from the same source, screen and sample position. A opaque card is the best supported choice for the stated goal. Use reader, chooser and reason-giver roles; no competition.

rows: Most light passes; faint edge visible
table.caption: Constructed teaching evidence

slides.prompt: W1. Which sample fits our design goal?
slides.reveal: A: the opaque card gave the clearest dark shape in these cases.

slides.title: The disappearing-shape challenge
body: The card moves out of the beam.
Predict what changes on the screen.
slides.notes: Let pupils move a card on a tabletop or use the case. A shadow from this card disappears from the tested screen area when it no longer blocks that path. Ask why a black and a red opaque card of equal shape can give similar silhouettes.
slides.reveal: Removing the blocker lets light reach that area again.

slides.title: Why is there a shadow?
body: Choose the account that follows the light.
slides.notes: If pupils choose dark paint, remove and return the card in the model. If source goes off, show the ray paths still reaching around the edges.

options.text: The card sends dark paint onto the screen.
options.feedback: No material travels from the card; some light paths are blocked.

options.text: The card blocks light, so less reaches part of the screen.
options.feedback: This is the shadow region; light can still reach around the card.

options.text: The source switches off when the card arrives.
options.feedback: The source can stay on. The card blocks only some paths.

slides.title: Choose your investigation route
slides.notes: Give one route only, selected with the pupil. The shared evidence page supports every route. Optional practical: test pre-cut samples at the fixed position, leaving the source and screen still. Record actual observations rather than copying sample results. If contrast is poor, use the supplied cases and discuss the limitation.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Read or point to one clue.
slides.notes: Shares the 12-minute independent stage. Optional practical: test pre-cut samples at the fixed position, leaving the source and screen still. Record actual observations rather than copying sample results. If contrast is poor, use the supplied cases and discuss the limitation.

slides.title: Make your own science record
body: Use a diagram, words or speech.
Check one answer with the evidence.
slides.notes: Allow ten minutes of independent response after the two-minute setup. Optional practical: test pre-cut samples at the fixed position, leaving the source and screen still. Record actual observations rather than copying sample results. If contrast is poor, use the supplied cases and discuss the limitation.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: Does my answer match the evidence?
slides.notes: Shares the independent stage. Ask the pupil to point to the clue supporting their answer; accept a spoken correction or changed choice.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve our account
body: Choose how to share one idea.
Use evidence to improve our account.
slides.notes: Give a private or paired option. Adopt one scientifically sound pupil revision in the class explanation and name the change. No public ranking.
slides.prompt: What is a shadow made of?
slides.reveal: It is not a substance: it is a region where less light reaches because light is blocked.

slides.title: Three quick checks
body: E1. What does an opaque card do to light?
E2. Where is the shadow in our setup?
E3. What changes when the card leaves the beam?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual answers. Secure core requires the main idea and a relevant reason. Revisit the relevant worked diagram next lesson if the explanation reverses cause and effect.
slides.reveal: See the teacher answer guide for the three checks.

pupilPages.title: Evidence: the screen test
pupilPages.intro: Constructed observations. Same source, screen and sample position in A–C.

cards.title: A • Opaque card
cards.text: A clear, dark shape is seen on the screen.

cards.title: B • Translucent paper
cards.text: Some light passes through. The shape is lighter and less distinct.

cards.title: C • Clear plastic
cards.text: Most light passes through. A faint edge is visible.

cards.title: D • Move the card away
cards.text: The source stays on. The opaque card moves fully out of this beam path.

blocks.prompt: W1. Choose A, B or C for a clear dark silhouette. Give a reason.
W2. Predict what D changes on the screen. Explain.

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Make a shadow plan
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: source / card / screen / blocks.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which sample best makes a dark silhouette here?
S2. Complete: The opaque card __ light.
S3. Put these in order: source / screen / card.
S4. Where do we see the shadow in this setup?
S5. Explain what happens when the card leaves the beam.

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Write the design record
pupilPages.intro: Use the observations, or add your own if a practical runs.

blocks.prompt: T2. Draw source, card and screen. Mark where light is blocked and where the shadow is.
T3. Explain why “clear plastic can never cast a shadow” is too strong.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Repair the display explanation
pupilPages.intro: A display says: “The black card paints a black copy of itself on the screen.”

blocks.prompt: X1. Replace this with a light-based explanation.
X2. Predict what a red opaque card of the same shape and size would do in the same position.
X3. Why might a shadow look grey rather than completely black in a classroom?
X4. Suggest a check that shows blocking, not coloured paint, causes the screen change.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. What does an opaque card do to light?
E2. Where is the shadow in our setup?
E3. What changes when the card leaves the beam?
R1. Which idea did you improve after hearing evidence?
R2. What would you investigate or ask next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 valid light source. 2 returns light from a surface. 3 yes, an opaque card stops light passing through.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 A; it has the clear dark shape in the evidence. W2 light reaches the tested screen area again, so that card’s shadow there disappears.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Second option correct. The card blocks some light paths; it does not send paint or switch off the source.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 A. S2 blocks. S3 source→card→screen. S4 on the screen. S5 light reaches the area again; that shadow disappears.

answers.label: T1–T3
answers.answer: T1 A blocks transmission and makes dark shape; B transmits some and scatters it; C transmits much light but can show a faint edge. T2 correct relative positions, blocking at the card, shadow behind it on screen. T3 the supplied clear sample has a faint visible edge; clear materials can redirect or reflect some light.

answers.label: X1–X4
answers.answer: X1 the opaque card blocks light, reducing light reaching part of the screen. X2 similar dark silhouette in this simple setup; the card’s red colour is not projected as a red picture. X3 room light or other reflected light can still reach the shadow area. X4 move card out and back while source stays on, or compare equal opaque shapes of different colours.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 blocks it from passing through. E2 on the screen behind the blocker relative to source. E3 light reaches that area again; the shadow from that blocker is removed.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a science-related revision or relevant next question. A pass or private response is acceptable; preferences have no fixed right answer.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 7; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 12; review 3; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the stage time.
BUILD follows the user’s Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful materials for secondary pupils. Routes are adjustable access choices, not fixed groups or diagnoses.
Every core task can run from the printed evidence. Do not present constructed teaching evidence as observations pupils made. A pupil’s spoken reasoning carries the same scientific value as writing.
Do not force the wording “no shadow” for a transparent sample. Clear materials reflect and refract some light; surface edges and imperfect transmission may create faint patterns.
Success rests on a causal explanation, not remembering the longest vocabulary word. Accept “does not let the light through” for opaque.

HTML We do: pupils choose a prediction, test it against the user-controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. The shared paper cases and W1/W2 prompts provide the equivalent classroom discussion without a device. Any animation is a teaching model, not filmed experimental evidence.
